text:
The high-pitched whine from the far corner of the cabin now intensified, no longer a mere hum but a fractured, strained chord that vibrated not just in his teeth, but in the marrow of his bones. The shadows there, deeper than the deepest night, began to pulse with a sickly internal light, a slow, deliberate beat like a monstrous, submerged heart. David still knelt, Iris’s wooden bird warm in his palm, its etched ‘7.17’ a tiny, terrible beacon in the gloom. He understood now: the numbers weren’t just markers; they were coordinates, a coded language of debt and collapse, and Iris, at seven years old, had been an early, unwilling cartographer. The Undertow wasn’t just an architect; it was a narrativist, and he, David Vance, was merely its pen, or perhaps, its page, turning over new revelations whether he willed it or not. The air around him grew heavy, smelling of ozone and spent circuitry, a phantom memory of a screen going dark, of a broadcast cutting out mid-sentence. 

As he pushed himself up, drawn by the pulsing darkness, a new manuscript page, brittle and curled at the edges, drifted down from a splintered ceiling beam, catching the phosphorescent glow. His eyes scanned the familiar type: *“Huang’s final public statement came not as words, but as a restructuring of reality itself, a therapy of absolute demolition. The architect, apologizing for structural infirmities, accepted the terms: a debt repaid in 718 foundational units, each one a memory unbuilt, a future rescinded.”* The page fluttered to the ash-stained floor, a chilling echo of the market’s cold equations. This wasn't therapy in any human sense; it was a cosmic repossession, Huang’s empire dismantled piece by excruciating piece, and in its place, the Undertow built its own, using the very ruins as its foundation.

The shadows in the corner coalesced further, not into a discernible figure, but into a section of the wall itself. The scorched timber, already peeling and decayed, began to ripple and flex, a slow, sickening undulation as if the structure were made of muscle and sinew, breathing with a shallow, ragged intake. A faint, low murmur emanated from it, a chorus of strained, resigned voices, repeating fragments of architectural terms and apologies in an unnervingly calm drone: *“...load-bearing compromised... unforgivable... a necessary correction...”* David’s gaze locked onto the flexing surface. There, impossibly, a faint, almost transparent handprint began to press out from the shifting wood, small and unmistakable, branded with the phantom outline of ‘7.17.’ Iris. She wasn't just gone; she was *here*, integrated, a part of the Undertow’s dreadful, architectural design.
